newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Christmas cookies cheer US sailors near trade talks.
newsitem.headline: Christmas cookies cheer US sailors near trade talks.

text.p: Neither trade barriers nor thousands of sea miles could stop an American mum sending her Navy son his favourite Christmas cookies -- all 700 pounds (320 kg) of them.

Andy Norton, a slightly pudgy 22-year-old technician on a U.S. destroyer, was overwhelmed on Thursday when told his mother and a townful of friends in tiny Elkhorn, Wisconsin, had baked the cookies for him and his shipmates 17,000 km (10,000 miles) away in equatorial Singapore.
"This is nuts, this is crazy. I am kind of surprised and embarrassed. This is unbelievable," Norton cried, turning crimson amid cheers of thanks from his 320 friends.
"It doesn't surprise me though. My mom is like that. But I didn't think she would get the whole town behind it," he said.
The sailors of the USS Paul Hamilton were at first bewildered when a third of a tonne of cookies and a brace of Singaporean girls dressed as elves landed on their deck.
Ship Commander William Landay had kept the surprise a close secret for more than a month.
"We are all away from our home and families since November, and these people whom we have never met have gone out of their way to do something. This is really neat, really great", he told Reuters.
Said Norton, chomping on a mouthful of chocolate chip: "I am a bit overweight and this is not helping very much but I like it anyway."
His mother has sent homemade cookies to him every Christmas throughout his three years in the service.
The great 1996 bake began when Mrs Norton gathered a few more mums to make enough cookies for some of her son's friends too.
Before they could cry "dough", mums from all over the town of 5,000 souls had gathered around in the spirit of Christmas to make enough for the entire ship.
Then they faced the problem of how to get the sackfuls of cookies half way across the world in time for Christmas.
But international courier company DHL read about their plight in a local newspaper and flew in the cookies for free.
The operation was a timely symbol of free trade as ministers from 128 countries haggled over dismantling trade barriers at the World Trade Organisation conference in central Singapore.

Said one sailor, chewing merrily: "The WTO is one of the finest institutions in the civilised world. It has brought more products into our country and enabled me, a common sailor, to go out and defend democracy for a few million more people."
